title: First Completely Painted Row or Column
statement:
`mat` is an `m x n` grid and `arr` is a list of length `m * n`; each of them holds every integer from `1` to `m * n` exactly once.

Walk through `arr` from index `0` onwards. At index `i`, colour the cell of `mat` whose value is `arr[i]`. Return the first index `i` at which, right after colouring, some row or some column of `mat` has all of its cells coloured.
constraints: the values of arr are distinct
the values of mat are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Re-scanning the whole grid after every step (or checking the coloured cell's entire row and column) would cost O(m · n · (m + n)). Two observations remove that work. First, a value's cell never moves, so a map from value to `[row, column]` answers "where is `arr[i]`?" in O(1). Second, a row is complete exactly when `cols` of its cells are coloured, so a counter per row and per column is all the state we need. Only the row and column of the newly coloured cell can become complete, so only those two counters need checking.

## Approach

1. Record `position`: each value of `mat` mapped to its `[r, c]`.
2. Keep `rowCount` (coloured cells per row) and `colCount` (coloured cells per column), all zero.
3. For each index `i`, look up `[r, c]` of `arr[i]` and add one to `rowCount[r]` and `colCount[c]`.
4. If `rowCount[r]` reached `cols` or `colCount[c]` reached `rows`, return `i`.

Every value is coloured by the end, so the loop always returns; the final `-1` is never reached.

## Example 1, step by step

`mat = [[1, 4], [2, 3]]`, so `position` maps `1 → [0, 0]`, `4 → [0, 1]`, `2 → [1, 0]`, `3 → [1, 1]`. At `i = 0` value `1` makes `rowCount = [1, 0]`, `colCount = [1, 0]`. At `i = 1` value `3` makes `rowCount = [1, 1]`, `colCount = [1, 1]`. At `i = 2` value `4` makes `rowCount[0] = 2 = cols`, so the answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n): building the map and the single pass over `arr` touch each value once.
- Space: O(m · n) for `position`, plus O(m + n) for the counters.

## Pitfalls

- A row is full when it has `cols` coloured cells, and a column when it has `rows`; swapping the two breaks non-square grids.
- With a single row or column, every cell completes a column (or row) by itself, so the answer is `0`.
- Return the index `i`, not the value `arr[i]`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rows`, `cols` | the grid's height `m` and width `n` |
| `position` | map from a value to its `[r, c]` in `mat` |
| `rowCount`, `colCount` | coloured cells in each row and column |
| `i` | current index in `arr` |
| `r`, `c` | cell of the value being coloured |
